--- Page 1 ---
AI Inference-Aware Optimal Power Flow:
Converting Token Requirements into Grid Flexibility
Qianyi Ma, Dawei Qiu
School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering
Nanyang Technological University
Singapore 639798, Singapore
qianyi.ma@ntu.edu.sg, dawei.qiu@ntu.edu.sg
Xiao Liu
College of Engineering
Cornell University
Ithaca, NY 14853, USA
xl2372@cornell.edu
Abstract—The rapid growth, temporal variability, and ge-
ographic concentration of electricity demand from artificial
intelligence (AI) inference can aggravate transmission congestion
near data centers (DCs). The spatial and temporal flexibility
of inference workloads offers an opportunity to alleviate this
congestion: requests can be routed across DCs or deferred
within users’ quality-of-service (QoS) requirements. However,
inference routing primarily considers graphics processing unit
(GPU) availability, leaving this flexibility underused in grid
operation. Using GPU measurements, this paper models inference
latency and DC power consumption to quantify the flexibility
available under users’ time-to-first-token (TTFT) and inter-token
latency (ITL) requirements. These models are then incorporated
into an AI inference-aware optimal power flow (OPF) that
coordinates inference routing and power system operation among
DC operators, the transmission system operator, and inference
users. By linking user requests, token generation at DCs, and
electricity delivery through the transmission network, the formu-
lation schedules inference workloads subject to both users’ QoS
requirements and transmission constraints. Simulations on the
PJM system show that, compared with computing-based routing
and with electricity price-based routing, coordinating inference
routing with network operation enables growing DC electricity
demand deliverable to be met at lower cost.
Index Terms—AI inference, data centers, demand flexibility,
optimal power flow, quality of service, tokens.
I. INTRODUCTION
Artificial intelligence (AI) inference accounts for an esti-
mated 80–90% of AI computing demand [1], and its continued
growth is expected to increase electricity consumption in data
centers (DCs) [2]. Inference load may be concentrated at a
small number of transmission buses and fluctuate with user
requests [3]. This concentration and variability can worsen
local transmission congestion and limit the additional DC load
that the network can supply.
At the same time, inference offers spatial and temporal flex-
ibility that could help relieve this congestion. Each inference
request generates a sequence of tokens, the basic units of
model output. Users’ quality-of-service (QoS) requirements
include limits on time-to-first-token (TTFT), the delay from
request submission to the first output token, and inter-token
latency (ITL), the interval between successive output tokens.
Requests can be routed among geographically distributed DCs
while respecting these latency limits. Users may also permit
requests to be completed within a specified deferral window
[4]. A field trial has demonstrated that DC electricity use can
be reduced during system peaks while maintaining workload-
level QoS [5].
In current practice, inference routing primarily considers
computing resources and communication latency. Cloud plat-
forms direct requests to DCs with available graphics process-
ing units (GPUs) and low communication latency [6], [7],
while deferrable requests are scheduled to use otherwise idle
GPUs [8]. These mechanisms do not explicitly account for
transmission constraints, leaving inference flexibility under-
used in power system operation.
Related research has approached inference flexibility from
two perspectives. From the computing perspective, studies
have explored serving requests across regions to reduce GPU
rental costs [9], adapting inference operation to electricity
prices [10], [11], and pricing inference services according to
latency requirements [12]. From the power system perspective,
DCs have been modeled as responsive electricity loads [13] or
spatially shiftable demand for emissions reduction [14], [15],
or participants in demand response programs [16], [17].
Each perspective captures only part of the interaction among
user requests, DC computing, and the power grid. Inference
serving decisions determine the location, timing, and magni-
tude of DC electricity demand. However, computing-oriented
studies often overlook how these decisions affect transmission
congestion, leaving available flexibility underused in grid
operation. Grid-oriented studies, in turn, may overestimate
this flexibility by neglecting user QoS requirements or DC
computing constraints. Two questions therefore remain: how
much DC flexibility the grid can actually use while satisfying
these requirements and constraints, and how inference serving
can be coordinated with network operation.
To answer these questions, the main contributions of this
paper are as follows:
1) An inference flexibility model is developed using GPU
measurements. It links token generation to DC power con-
sumption and quantifies the flexibility available to the grid
under users’ TTFT limits, ITL limits, and request deferral
windows.
2) An AI inference-aware OPF is proposed to coordinate
inference routing and power system operation among the
transmission system operator, DC operators, and inference
users. It links user requests and token generation at DCs
with electricity delivery through the transmission network
under QoS, computing, and transmission constraints.

II. AI INFERENCE-AWARE OPF FRAMEWORK
Fig. 1 illustrates the coordinated operation among infer-
ence platforms, DC operators, and the transmission system
operator. DC operators provide information on their installed
model replicas and the measured relationship among replica
throughput, latency, and GPU power consumption. Here, a
replica denotes one copy of an AI model deployed on a
specified group of GPUs. Inference platforms aggregate user
requests by geographic region and QoS class, and provide
the corresponding token demand, TTFT and ITL limits, and
permissible deferral windows. The proposed AI inference-
aware OPF uses these data as inputs together with generation
offers and transmission network constraints.
These inputs constrain where and when inference requests
can be served and how many tokens each active replica can
produce. Specifically, the TTFT limit restricts which DCs can
serve requests from each user region. The ITL requirement
limits how many tokens an active replica can produce per
hour. The deferral window specifies when demand may be
served. Subject to these limits and transmission constraints,
the inference-aware OPF selects where and when tokens are
produced, how many replicas are activated, and how generators
are dispatched.
These latency and deferral requirements vary across infer-
ence applications. The model therefore considers two request
classes. Interactive requests, such as conversational inference,
cannot be deferred and require a relatively fast token stream.
Flexible requests, such as batch inference jobs, allow a slower
token stream and may be deferred within a specified window.
The OPF uses hourly intervals to represent deferral across
hours. Inference platforms implement the resulting token allo-
cations by routing and scheduling individual requests within
each hour.
III. AI INFERENCE-AWARE OPF MODEL
The system operator maximizes social welfare, i.e., the
utility of the served inference demand minus the generation
cost. Since all demand must be served, this utility is fixed, and
the problem reduces to minimizing the total generation cost
over the hours t ∈T , subject to the request constraints (2)–
(4), the DC constraints (5)–(8), and the network constraints
(9)–(12):

B. Data Center Model
Each DC i hosts a fixed number wi replicas. In hour t, xi,s,t
of replicas are activated for QoS class s, and the others remain
idle. The variable xi,s,t is continuous, which allows replicas
to be shared within an hour. A replica raises its throughput
v, i.e., its token generation rate, by serving more requests
concurrently, at the expense of a longer ITL. Fig. 2 captures
this trade-off with an increasing ITL curve Li(v) and an affine
GPU power fit ai+βiv. The ITL limit of class s therefore caps
the throughput of a replica at ¯vi,s, defined by Li(¯vi,s) = ¯LITL
s
,
so that a replica produces at most ¯Ri,s = κ¯vi,s class-s tokens
in an hourly interval of κ seconds. The class-s token output

an activation component proportional to the number of active
replicas, and a token-production component proportional to
token output. A tighter ITL limit can reduce the token capacity
of each replica. Serving the same token demand may therefore
require more active replicas, increasing the activation overhead
and hence the average energy consumption per token.
C. Transmission Network Constraints
DC i draws pi,t at bus n(i) of a network with buses n ∈N,
lines ℓ∈L, and generators k ∈K. Under the direct-current
power-flow approximation, with other load Loth

eration with the DC load and the other load. Constraint (10)
keeps the line flows, obtained from the net bus injections (11)
through the power transfer distribution factors, within their
limits. Finally, constraint (12) bounds the generator outputs.
In summary, the decision variables are the generator outputs
g, the deferral schedule z, the token routing y, and the DC
token outputs r and active replicas x. And the proposed OPF
is a convex program.
IV. CASE STUDIES
Case studies use the 7,830-bus PJM network [18]. Solar pro-
files are derived from the National Solar Radiation Database
[19], wind profiles from bias-corrected High-Resolution Rapid
Refresh data [20], and load profiles from EIA-930 [21]. A total
of 333 DCs are identified from public inventories, including
the IM3 atlas [22], and mapped to 138 buses. Fig. 3 shows the
resulting test system. The main DC clusters are in Northern
Virginia (DOM), Ohio (AEP), and the Chicago area (ComEd).
At each DC, 10% of capacity is allocated to infer-
ence. Each replica serves Llama-3.1-405B on eight H100
GPUs, with serving curves fitted to measurements from the
ML.ENERGY Benchmark [23]. Requests originate from three
regions: Chicago, Northern Virginia, and New Jersey. RTTs are
obtained from RIPE Atlas [24], and request demand profiles
from BurstGPT [3]. The median ITL limits are 36.3 ms for
interactive requests and 48.0 ms for flexible requests. Both
classes have an 80-ms TTFT limit, with a 40-ms prefill time.
Weekly simulations cover July 10–16, 2023, with cyclic
hour indexing so that deferral windows wrap around the end
of the week. Single-hour analyses use the snapshot at 16:00
on July 15, 2023. All optimization models are solved using
Gurobi 12.0.3.
A. Superiority of the Inference-Aware OPF
To evaluate the benefit of coordinating inference routing
with network operation, the proposed OPF is compared with
two routing benchmarks: 1) Computing-based routing (pre-
vailing industry practice) assigns each request to the nearest
reachable DC, i.e., the one with the lowest RTT, among
those with spare GPU capacity [6], [7]; 2) Ex-ante LMP-
based routing assigns each request to the reachable DC with
the lowest electricity cost per token, evaluated using LMPs
computed without inference load, and routes excess demand
to the next cheapest reachable DC [17]. GPU capacity and
token demand are scaled at the existing DC buses to obtain
inference energy shares of 2–8%.
Table I reports the number of network-infeasible hours and
the weekly system cost added by inference. Relative cost
increases are calculated using the inference-aware OPF with
a 12-h deferral window as the reference. At low inference
shares, when both benchmarks remain feasible, computing-
based routing yields the highest cost, followed by LMP-based
routing. Computing-based routing minimizes latency without
considering electricity prices. LMP-based routing uses prices
and respects GPU capacity limits, but does not jointly consider
the alternative DCs available to different user regions. It may
therefore assign scarce low-cost capacity to requests with
other affordable options, leaving requests with fewer options
to be served at expensive DCs. The proposed OPF instead

jointly optimizes routing and GPU allocation, reserving low-
cost capacity to requests with fewer affordable alternatives and
directing requests with more options elsewhere. This reduces
reliance on expensive DCs and lowers the overall system cost.
At inference shares of 6% and 8%, both benchmark
schemes become network-infeasible during weekday after-
noons, whereas the proposed OPF remains feasible in every
hour. Under computing-based routing, requests from Northern
Virginia concentrate at nearby DCs in the DOM zone, where
the additional load exceeds the zone’s available import ca-
pability. LMP-based routing produces fewer infeasible hours
but also concentrates demand at low-price DCs, since its
routing prices do not reflect the additional congestion caused
by inference load. The proposed OPF avoids these violations
by routing part of the demand to DCs in Ohio and western
Pennsylvania that remain reachable within the users’ TTFT
limits. Allowing deferral further reduces the system cost,
although the percentage savings decline as the inference share
increases. This is because the additional demand shifted to
night-time hours raises LMPs in those hours, reducing the
savings from off-peak operation.
Fig. 4 compares nodal LMPs under LMP-based routing
and the proposed OPF for the single-hour snapshot at an 8%
inference energy share. The proposed OPF routes part of the
inference demand to northern areas where exports of local
generation are constrained, allowing more generation to be
consumed locally. LMPs there rise from negative levels, while
those in the high-price eastern areas decline. This reallocation
narrows the spatial spread of LMPs, and congestion rent also
falls without network reinforcement.

B. Sensitivity Analysis of Inference Requirements
Fig. 5 shows how system cost changes when the TTFT and
ITL limits are relaxed separately, with all other parameters
held fixed. In Fig. 5(a), relaxing the TTFT limit makes
additional DCs reachable, reducing system cost in steps. Once
the low-cost DCs are reachable from every user region, further
relaxation no longer reduces cost. In Fig. 5(b), relaxing the
ITL limit reduces both system cost and the number of active
replicas serving interactive requests. A looser ITL limit allows
each replica to serve more requests at once. The same demand
can therefore be served with fewer active replicas, reducing
activation power.
In summary, the two limits affect system cost through
different mechanisms: relaxing TTFT expands the choice of
serving locations, whereas relaxing ITL increases the token
capacity of each replica and reduces the associated activation
overhead. Over the tested ranges, system cost is more sensitive
to the ITL limit than to the TTFT limit. The comparison
highlights the value of inference-serving efficiency as a source
of grid flexibility.
C. Temporal Flexibility of Inference
Fig. 6(a) the arrivals and service of flexible tokens under a
12-h deferral window. Deferral shifts afternoon arrivals into
the night, when LMPs are low and GPUs are idle, which
lowers both the generation cost and the DC load at the daily
PJM peak. As the PJM night load rises on Thursday and
Friday, fewer cheap hours remain, and the deferred demand
concentrates into sharp night peaks.

Fig. 6. Temporal flexibility of inference: (a) flexible-token service and PJM
load under the 12-h deferral window; (b) DC load and cost saving versus
deferral window.
Fig. 6(b) shows how the length of the deferral window
affects the weekly saving and the DC load. Short windows
already shift the afternoon arrivals away from the system
peak, so the DC load at that peak stops declining once
the window reaches 6 h. Weekly savings continue to grow,
however, as longer windows allow demand to be served during
the cheapest night hours. With long windows, deferred demand
concentrates into sufficiently few hours that peak DC load
exceeds its level without deferral. Longer windows therefore
provide additional cost savings but can increase night DC
peaks, which remain subject to the transmission constraints
enforced by the OPF.
V. CONCLUSION
This paper proposed an AI inference-aware OPF that jointly
determines inference routing, replica activation, and generator
dispatch under users’ QoS requirements and transmission
constraints. Case studies on the PJM system show that this
coordination enables growing DC electricity demand to be met
at lower operating cost on the existing transmission network.
Users’ latency tolerance provides flexibility by expanding
routing options and increasing the token capacity of each
replica, thereby reducing activation overhead. Longer deferral
windows yield further savings but can concentrate demand into
higher night-time peaks at DC buses. By incorporating users’
latency and deferral limits as explicit optimization constraints,
the framework provides a basis for inference platforms to offer
grid-responsive services.
